story|title:don t go monolithic the agen.content_excerpt: The defensible asset in enterprise AI is not the model. It’s the organizational world model. Every major compute era decomposes into specialized layers with different winners at each level. Cloud split into IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. The modern data stack split into ingestion, warehousing, transformation, and BI. Each time, specialists beat the generalists because each layer has its own economics: its own rate of change, capital requirements, and sources of lock-in. The enterprise AI agent stack is doing the same thing right now. Arvind Jain, the CEO of Glean, recently published a structural analysis of the emerging enterprise agent architecture that crystallized something I’d been thinking about. He describes a stack splitting into six layers (security, context, models, orchestration, agents, and interfaces), and each layer is defensible to a different degree. Glean sits in the context layer so the usual positioning caveats apply, but the structural argument is sound regardless of who makes it. The three sections below cover models converging toward shared infrastructure, the two depths of the context layer, and the compounding flywheel that context and orchestration form. The model layer is converging fastest toward commodity economics. Training costs scale roughly 2.4x per year , with current frontier runs costing hundreds of millions and billion-dollar training runs already underway , according to Anthropic’s Dario Amodei. Only a handful of organizations on Earth can operate at this scale: OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta, and a few others including xAI and Mistral. This is capital-intensive infrastructure, with the same structure as semiconductor fabs or cloud hyperscalers. I expect foundation models to become shared utilities, so no enterprise will build a moat on one. Companies already act on this. 37% of enterprises now use five or more models in production , up from 29% the prior year. Different tasks demand different models: Claude for code and tool use, GPT for extended reasoning, Gemini Flash for low-latency routing, specialized models for image generation and embeddings. Betting your enterprise stack on a single model provider carries the same risk as betting it on a single cloud. Open standards like Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol , now hosted by the Linux Foundation with 97 million monthly SDK downloads, and Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol are making this multi-model enterprise AI architecture practical. story|title:neon and mubit an agent that.content_excerpt: An agent on Neon Functions, Lakebase Postgres, and AI Gateway that hands its routine steps to a small model tuned on its own traffic Mubit is middleware for AI agents. It sits between your agent and the model with a one-line endpoint change, learns from every call, and moves recurring steps to small models tuned on your own traffic, while the frontier model keeps the hard ones. There's nothing extra to host. To show how that works with Neon, they built a template for cutting frontier-model token spend - an agent on Neon Functions and Lakebase Postgres that sends every model call through Mubit to Neon AI Gateway . The example workload is a data analyst agent that answers business questions over Postgres, but the setup applies to any agent on Neon that calls frontier models through AI Gateway: Once Mubit has tuned a small model for the routine steps, it serves them itself, and lessons from verified runs help the agent avoid repeating mistakes. In the example workload, using Mubit cut the agent's gpt-5.5 tokens by 73% and made it 40% faster, without losing accuracy. "Neon gives agents a database and a model endpoint in one place. Mubit sits in between and learns from every call, so an agent on Neon gets cheaper and more reliable the more it runs" — Anil Peri, CEO at Mubit "We built AI Gateway so agents on Neon can call frontier models through one endpoint. Mubit is a good example of what you can put in front of it. The agent passes the repetitive stuff to small models, and when your schema changes, it drops what's out of date and figures out the new tables on its own" — Bryan Clark, Product Lead at Databricks Teams often build an agent on a frontier model and send every call to it. That's quite inefficient token-wise - cost and latency grow with every step, and a lot of those steps are routine - you end up paying frontier prices for work that doesn't need a frontier model. Mubit measured this with the template's example agent. On their benchmark, gpt-5.5 alone needed about 10 model calls, 21.7k gpt-5.5 input tokens, and 26 seconds to answer one question. Most of those calls were mechanical, like listing tables, reading table definitions, and writing up an answer the query had already found. Only the SQL steps actually needed the frontier model. Agents also don't remember what they've learned. story|title:sandbox resourcing burst don.content_excerpt: Across Modal, a typical Sandbox spends more than half its life using less than 6% of its peak CPU. Take a coding agent: the Sandbox sits nearly idle while the model reasons about what to do next, and spikes only when the agent installs dependencies, runs tests, or builds the project. The same pattern shows up in other common Sandbox workloads: RL rollouts, evals, and app builders. Today, most sandboxes are priced based on a fixed-resource reservation model. Reservations are a poor fit for spiky work, for two reasons: We believe your bill should align with your workload, rising when it’s busy and falling when it’s idle. That’s why our Sandboxes burst: a Sandbox gets the CPU and memory it needs when your work spikes and gives them back when it is done. You pay for what you actually use. Every Sandbox bursts by default. Start with the base 0.125 cores and 128 MiB request and let your Sandbox grow as it needs. With active-resource pricing, you pay each second for what you use, with the small request as a floor. You can request more to guarantee it, but you’ll pay for those resources even when your Sandbox is idle. You can also set a limit to cap how far your Sandbox can burst; think of it as setting the size of the computer the Sandbox lives on. Most workloads don’t need to set a request or limit: use the default and burst from there. Because you pay for what you use, estimate your costs from average usage rather than peak usage: CPU cost ≈ runtime × CPU rate × average cores used Memory cost ≈ runtime × memory rate × average GiB used This average works for bursting Sandboxes because each second, a Sandbox is billed for the higher of its request and what it actually uses. Since the average sits well below the peak, customers with bursty workloads can end up paying a fraction of their typical reservation bill. Your Sandbox is guaranteed its request, which is small by default. When it bursts beyond that, it draws from a shared pool of the machine’s idle capacity, which Modal’s scheduler keeps free on every machine. It works because of the law of averages. Sandboxes sharing a machine mostly run unrelated work for different customers, so they rarely spike at the same moment. If every Sandbox reserved capacity for its peak, the machine would need room for the sum of all the peaks. With bursting, it only needs room for the most they use at the same time. It’s the same reason a power grid can be much smaller than the sum of every household’s peak demand. For most work

story|title:security flaws in popular ai.content_excerpt: Reported security flaws in 17 popular open-source AI tools, including Open WebUI, Flowise, vLLM, and LangChain, jumped from 156 in all of 2025 to 423 in 2026 through October 28. Of the 133 flaws rated critical since 2023, 72 let an attacker run their own code on the server. These are tools teams install to run their own chatbots and AI workflows, often before security has reviewed them, so they need the same inventory, access controls, and patching as any other software. Open-source AI tools have become the default starting point for companies that want to run their own models, build an internal chatbot, or connect AI to their own documents. Most of them install in minutes. We wanted to know what security risk comes with them, so we counted. We pulled every security advisory GitHub has reviewed for 17 widely used open-source AI tools, published from January 2023 through October 28, 2026. The list covers interfaces for chatting with models (Open WebUI), servers for running them (Ollama, vLLM, SGLang), frameworks for connecting them to data (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack), visual workflow builders (Flowise, Langflow), and the infrastructure around them (LiteLLM, MLflow, Ray, BentoML, and others). That came to 737 advisories. Each one includes a publication date, a severity rating, and the type of weakness involved. Reported flaws nearly tripled in 2026. There were 156 advisories across these tools in all of 2025 and 423 from January through October 28, 2026. Critical flaws often mean full control of the server. 133 advisories were rated critical. 72 of those allow an attacker to run their own code on the machine running the tool. These servers commonly hold API keys, the documents the AI was given, and network access to internal systems. Four tools account for most of the total. Open WebUI (161), Flowise (114), vLLM (89), and MLflow (86) make up 61% of all advisories. They are also among the most widely deployed tools on the list. The weaknesses are familiar ones. The most common types were weak or missing access control (180 advisories), letting an attacker run code (147), and reading or writing files outside the intended scope (87). These are long-standing web application problems, not new AI-specific attacks. An increase in reported flaws is not proof that the software got worse. story|ver:145|title:edge0 145b frontier.content_excerpt: Today, we're open-sourcing Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B , together with our unified inference framework and deployment tools. Edge0-145B is the world's first open-source on-device AI model with 145 billion parameters. It brings coding, reasoning, and agent capabilities that rival frontier cloud models to your own computer. On-device AI has long forced a tradeoff between model capability and what the hardware can run. Larger models demand more memory, bandwidth, and power; smaller models can struggle with complex work. Moving that work to the cloud adds model-provider fees, data-handling constraints, and a dependence on connectivity. We're releasing the full stack so developers can reproduce the results, evaluate or fine-tune the models, and integrate them into their own products. Get the model weights , explore the inference framework , or try the Edge0 App . Edge0-145B makes a 145-billion-parameter model usable on a personal laptop. A useful local model has to fit in memory, process prompts promptly, generate fast enough to use, and keep power consumption under control. It also needs to sustain longer tasks. Our earlier Edge0-35B phone release reported peak memory below 2.5GB. On an iPhone 18 Pro Max, Edge0-35B delivers 37+ tokens/s using approximately 2.5GB of memory. Edge0-145B has roughly four times as many parameters; its laptop comparison reports 80+ tokens/s and 28GB peak memory. These measurements apply to different models and hardware. On-device model scale over time. The chart covers 67 open models of at least 1B parameters from 14 labs, intended for phones, laptops, and AI PCs. Same-size base, instruct, and reasoning variants count once; each line tracks a lab's largest model, including releases before July 2025. Filled points mark new highs and hollow points other releases. The scale is logarithmic below 40B and linear above it. Apple is excluded because its weights are not released. Sources: vendor announcements and model cards. Memory limits kept most on-device models below 10B parameters before September 2026.
